summary: A note from Alex McKenzie at BBN with network traffic statistics for July 1972. BBN had given ARPA a monthly summary of host packets output and, after requests, agreed to publish them as RFCs. The figures are monthly totals or overall averages. It was replaced by RFC 391.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a monthly tally from the early internet, showing how many packets each computer sent. Think of counting how many letters each house mailed in a month, so the post office can see where the traffic is.

questions: how much traffic did each arpanet host send
subtitle: Monthly statistics on ARPANET host data traffic for July 1972.

tldr.problem: ARPA and the ARPANET community needed visibility into how much traffic different hosts were generating to understand network usage patterns and capacity requirements.
tldr.mechanism: BBN collected monthly statistics on packets output by each host, distinguishing between inter-node traffic (between different hosts) and intra-node traffic (within the same host). They reported overall totals and daily averages.
tldr.outcome: This became a regular monthly reporting practice, with July 1972 showing UCLA and MIT hosts as the highest traffic generators, ranging from under 100 packets to over 3 million packets for some hosts during the month.

today: RFC 378 was replaced by RFC 391 as monthly traffic reporting continued. This snapshot of July 1972 shows the ARPANET when it had about 20 sites and was transitioning from experimental research project to operational network. Similar network traffic statistics remain central to network operations and capacity planning today.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Alex McKenzie at BBN reports on ARPANET traffic statistics for July 1972. BBN had been providing ARPA with monthly summaries of host packet output for several months. After requests from various sites, ARPA approved publishing these statistics as RFCs to give the broader network community visibility into traffic patterns.

The statistics count packets output from each host during July, distinguishing between inter-node traffic (packets sent to other hosts across the network) and intra-node traffic (packets used within a single host's processing).
sections.plainLanguage: BBN counted how many packets each computer sent out in July, either to other computers or to itself. They published these numbers so everyone could see the network's busiest spots.

sections.title: Traffic Data and Interpretation
sections.content:
The report provides monthly totals and daily averages for each host across the network. Notably, the figures represent either monthly totals or 24-hour averages, so they do not show peak traffic conditions. MIT Host 3 generated the highest inter-node traffic in July with 3.4 million packets, while UCLA Host 2 generated 1.2 million packets and Rand Host 2 generated 3.9 million packets.

Some sites like CASE had very light traffic (just 62 total packets), while others like McCleod had no traffic at all. The report also tracks the average number of packets per message sent between different hosts, showing it was 1.09 in July.
sections.plainLanguage: MIT and UCLA had the most traffic. Some computers barely used the network at all. The network moved about one extra packet per message on average.

sections.title: Network Usage Insights
sections.content:
The statistics reveal the usage patterns of early ARPANET: MIT, UCLA, and Rand were the heavy users, while many other sites generated minimal traffic. The split between inter-node and intra-node traffic shows which sites were using the network for actual inter-host communication versus local processing.

Total monthly traffic across all hosts exceeded 28 million packets, representing an average of about 502,000 inter-node packets per day across the entire network. These figures help explain why the ARPANET community was concerned with network reliability and performance.
sections.plainLanguage: MIT, UCLA, and Rand were the network's busy places. All together, the network moved about 28 million packets in July. The measurements showed the network was growing and getting real use.
